title: Equilibrium prices under hidden Markov fundamentals

paper.title: Equilibrium prices under hidden Markov fundamentals
paper.abstract: Abstract We study a representative-agent Epstein–Zin economy with geometric dividends and a hidden finite-state Markov drift. We allow the price–dividend ratio to contain an additional positive, absolutely continuous valuation factor and, within the class ℭ \mathfrak{C} defined below and under the regularity, admissibility, and positivity conditions of our main theorem, equilibrium forces this factor to be constant, yielding belief–Markovian prices. In the two-state case, under the stated positivity condition and strictly positive transition intensities, we prove existence, uniqueness, endpoint smoothness, interior analyticity, and uniform bounds for the positive solution of the pricing equation. For 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 , this solution supports an equilibrium under any continuous short rate satisfying the model’s one-sided portfolio condition. Finally, in the two-state subregion η > 0 \eta>0 , we derive belief-dependent stock volatility, a European option-pricing PDE, and a leading short-maturity conditional risk-neutral log-return skewness expansion.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Asset prices depend not only on current cash flows, but also on what investors believe about economic fundamentals that they cannot observe directly. When investors learn over time and have recursive preferences, it is not obvious whether current dividends and beliefs are enough to determine equilibrium prices or whether other price components may also arise. We study this question in a continuous-time model. Aggregate dividends satisfy d ​ D t D t = g t ​ d ​ t + σ ​ d ​ W t , \frac{\mathrm{d}D_{t}}{D_{t}}=g_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\mathrm{d}W_{t}, where W W is a Brownian motion, σ > 0 \sigma>0 is constant, and g g is an unobserved finite-state Markov chain driving the different states the economy can be in. The agent learns about the current growth regime from dividend observations. Investors observe only dividends, and thus we write 𝔽 D = ( ℱ t D ) t ≥ 0 \mathbb{F}^{\text{$D$}}=(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}})_{t\geq 0} for the completion of the natural filtration of D D . The representative agent has infinite-horizon Epstein–Zin preferences over consumption. That is, for a consumption process c c , the corresponding continuation utility V c V^{c} satisfies the recursive equation V t c = δ ​ θ 1 − γ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ∫ t + ∞ e − δ ​ θ ​ ( s − t ) ​ c s 1 − 1 / ψ ​ ( ( 1 − γ ) ​ V s c ) 1 − 1 / θ ​ 𝑑 s | ℱ t D ] , t ≥ 0 , V_{t}^{c}=\frac{\delta\theta}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{t}^{\text{$+$}\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\delta\theta(s-t)}c_{s}^{1-1/\psi}\big((1-\gamma)V_{s}^{c}\big)^{1-1/\theta}\mathrm{d}s\bigg|\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}}\bigg],\;t\geq 0, where δ > 0 \delta>0 is the discount rate, γ \gamma is the relative risk aversion, and ψ \psi is the intertemporal elasticity of substitution. Their interaction is summarised by θ ≔ 1 − γ 1 − ψ − 1 , \theta\coloneqq\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\psi^{-1}}, a parameter which will turn out to be qualitatively crucial for our results. Our paper first relates to the literature on learning and incomplete information in asset pricing. Detemple [ 15 ] provides an early general-equilibrium analysis in which investors filter an unobserved state, and Pástor and Veronesi [ 33 ] survey the broader learning literature. Our closest time-additive antecedents are Veronesi [ 39 , 40 ] , and David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . The closest recursive hidden-regime benchmarks are Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] and Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] . Veronesi [ 39 ] studies two unobserved dividend-growth regimes with additive dividends and CARA preferences. The equilibrium stock price is increasing and convex in the posterior probability of the high-growth state. Consequently, bad news in good times has a larger price effect than comparable good news in bad times, while learning also generates belief-dependent return volatility. This belief-driven asymmetry motivates our analysis of the shape of the price–dividend ratio. A closer time-additive benchmark for our pure-exchange and geometric-dividend setting is Veronesi [ 40 ] . That paper considers finitely many hidden growth states under time-additive isoelastic preferences and derives an affine price–dividend ratio in posterior beliefs. Its main question is how the quality of investors’ information affects risk premia and stock-return moments. David and Veronesi [ 14 ] provide the closest pure-diffusion option-pricing benchmark. They consider lognormal fundamentals and finitely many hidden regimes under time-additive isoelastic preferences. Their price–dividend ratio is affine in posterior beliefs, and they show how the common innovation to fundamentals and beliefs generates belief-dependent stochastic volatility, a changing return–volatility covariance, a market price of belief risk, and time variation in option-implied distributions. For two states, they also develop a Fourier option-pricing method. Learning-generated option skews also precede our analysis. Guidolin and Timmermann [ 23 ] derive closed-form European option prices in an equilibrium model in which the probabilities governing dividend news are unknown and updated recursively. They show that Bayesian learning can generate asymmetric implied-volatility skews and systematic patterns across maturities. These learning, volatility, and option-pricing channels are therefore not new to our paper. The second ingredient we use is recursive utility. Epstein–Zin preferences originate with Epstein and Zin [ 18 ] , while Duffie and Epstein [ 16 ] provide the continuous-time stochastic differential utility formulation used here. Weil [ 41 ] and Epstein and Zin [ 19 ] study the asset-pricing implications of separating risk aversion from intertemporal substitution. Epstein–Zin preferences have already been combined with learning about hidden regimes. Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] study a discrete-time Lucas-tree economy with a hidden finite-state endowment regime, Bayesian and distorted learning rules, and Epstein–Zin preferences. Their equilibrium price–dividend ratio satisfies a generally nonlinear expectation equation and is computed as a function of posterior beliefs. Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] consider a hidden two-state economy with an additional noisy signal and focus on how information quality affects expected returns. They obtain the price–consumption ratio w ⁡ ( p ) = ( p ​ w b κ + ( 1 − p ) ​ w r κ ) 1 / κ , w(p)=\big(pw_{b}^{\kappa}+(1-p)w_{r}^{\kappa}\big)^{1/\kappa}, which is also the price–dividend ratio in their endowment economy. Their parameter κ = 1 − γ 1 − ψ − 1 , \kappa=\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\psi^{-1}}, is the counterpart of our θ \theta . They show that this ratio is strictly convex in the belief when κ < 1 \kappa<1 and strictly concave when κ > 1 \kappa>1 . Related work by Ju and Miao [ 29 ] combines learning about hidden Markov growth regimes with generalised recursive smooth-ambiguity preferences. Relative to Veronesi [ 39 ] , David and Veronesi [ 14 ] , Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] , and Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] , our contribution goes in several directions. The continuous-time Epstein–Zin aggregator used here separates risk aversion from intertemporal substitution and leads, away from θ = 1 \theta=1 , to a generally nonlinear pricing equation on the belief simplex. The nonlinearity itself is not new in view of the preceding recursive-utility models. Our first contribution is instead to study whether the belief–Markovian representation used in those models can be obtained as an equilibrium conclusion when a further valuation state is allowed at the outset. More specifically, the earlier papers work with belief-Markovian price representations, whereas we begin with a broader class in which the price–dividend ratio may contain an additional finite-variation valuation state and may therefore retain information about the history of beliefs. We consider a class ℭ \mathfrak{C} of candidate systems which, for every initial belief p p , generate a stock price of the form S t p = D t p ​ H t p ​ φ ​ ( P t p ) , t ≥ 0 , H 0 p = h ⁡ ( p ) , S_{t}^{p}=D_{t}^{p}H_{t}^{p}{\varphi(P_{t}^{p})},\;t\geq 0,\;H_{\text{$0$}}^{p}=h(p), where P p P^{p} is the posterior-belief process, φ \varphi is a positive function on the simplex, and H p H^{p} is a positive, absolutely continuous valuation factor. The term φ ⁡ ( P t p ) \varphi(P_{t}^{p}) captures the effect of current beliefs, whereas H t p H_{t}^{p} may be path-dependent. The class ℭ \mathfrak{C} is broader than a belief–Markovian specification, but it does not contain arbitrary adapted path-dependent prices. The process H p H^{p} must be the unique global positive solution of an ordinary differential equation driven by ( P p , H p ) (P^{p},H^{p}) , and the Borel maps generating H p H^{p} and the short rate are common to all initial-belief model copies. We call a candidate a ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium when, for every p p , the representative agent holds the outstanding stock, holds no risk-free asset in net supply, and consumes the dividend, as in Veronesi [ 39 ] and David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . Our main result shows that, under the regularity, admissibility, and positivity conditions of Theorem 3.1 , including a classical C 2 C^{2} state representation of the agent’s value function, equilibrium eliminates the apparent additional freedom. Even when h h is assumed only Borel measurable, there is a constant h 0 > 0 h_{\text{$0$}}>0 such that h ⁡ ( p ) = h 0 , H t p = h 0 , t ≥ 0 , h(p)=h_{\text{$0$}},\;H_{t}^{p}=h_{\text{$0$}},\;t\geq 0, for every initial belief. Hence, the stock price is Markovian in dividends and posterior beliefs. The belief–Markovian representation used in the earlier literature is therefore an equilibrium conclusion within ℭ \mathfrak{C} , not an assumption. This conclusion is deliberately stated within ℭ \mathfrak{C} : it does not assert that every conceivable adapted equilibrium price, or every solution of an infinite-horizon recursive valuation equation, must be belief–Markovian. This question is related to the literature on existence and uniqueness in infinite-horizon recursive models. More broadly, Santos and Woodford [ 35 ] give conditions that rule out rational asset-pricing bubbles in infinite-horizon economies. Borovička and Stachurski [ 5 , 6 ] derive necessary and sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness in classes of discrete-time recursive-utility and equilibrium asset-pricing problems. Pohl, Schmedders and Wilms [ 34 ] study recursive wealth–consumption ratios, including applications with learning, and select the limit of finite-horizon solutions, which they characterise as the unique homogeneous solution without a bubble. These papers show why the existence of a stationary pricing equation does not, by itself, settle the economic selection problem. Our result addresses a different and more specific question: equilibrium and admissibility eliminate the additional absolutely continuous state admitted by ℭ \mathfrak{C} in the present continuous-time hidden-regime economy. Second, once the belief-Markovian representation is established, we derive the pricing equation for any finite number of hidden regimes and analyse it in detail in the two-state case. The resulting boundary-value problem is degenerate at the endpoints of the belief interval. Under the stated positivity condition and strictly positive transition intensities, we prove existence and uniqueness of its positive classical solution for every θ > 0 \theta>0 . We further prove that the solution is uniformly bounded above and away from zero, smooth on the closed belief interval, and real analytic in its interior. For 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 , the two-state solution supports a ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium under any continuous short-rate specification satisfying the one-sided portfolio bound. This condition does not select a unique short rate. The direction and curvature of the belief response must also be distinguished. Denoting by g 1 g^{\text{$1$}} and g 2 g^{\text{$2$}} the high- and low-growth states, respectively, monotonicity is governed by η ≔ ( 1 − γ ) ​ ( g 1 − g 2 ) , \eta\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\big(g^{\text{$1$}}-g^{\text{$2$}}\big), the price–dividend ratio is increasing when η > 0 \eta>0 and decreasing when η < 0 \eta<0 . Curvature depends on θ \theta and on an additional sufficient condition. When the latter holds, the ratio is convex for 0 < θ < 1 0<\theta<1 and concave for θ > 1 \theta>1 , while for θ = 1 \theta=1 it is affine without this additional condition. The increasing–convex case echoes the qualitative news asymmetry of Veronesi [ 39 ] , while θ = 1 \theta=1 yields an affine belief dependence analogous to that in David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . As explained above, Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] already identify the corresponding preference-dependent change in curvature in discrete time; our contribution is the global existence, uniqueness, endpoint regularity, and shape analysis of the continuous-time degenerate boundary-value problem, together with its connection to the equilibrium-selection result. The maintained equilibrium analysis covers 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 . We do not analyse θ < 0 \theta<0 , which includes the often-used parameter combination γ > 1 \gamma>1 and ψ > 1 \psi>1 . We study θ > 1 \theta>1 at the level of the positive solution of the Markovian pricing equation, but do not provide the additional recursive-utility selection rule required to give those results an equilibrium interpretation. A further related literature combines recursive preferences and option pricing. Garcia, Luger and Renault [ 21 ] develop and estimate an Epstein–Zin option-pricing model with Markov latent variables, stochastic volatility, and time-varying skewness. The state history enters the information set on which their Euler equations are conditioned, so their latent-variable specification is not the same Bayesian filtering problem as ours. Benzoni, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein [ 3 ] study a continuous-time Epstein–Zin equilibrium in which investors update beliefs about a hidden regime governing rare-jump risk. Their mechanism generates changes in stock valuations and in the implied-volatility smirk. Finally, in the two-state subregion η > 0 \eta>0 (equivalently, γ < 1 \gamma<1 ), with the short rate set to its marginal upper bound and under the stated martingale and regularity conditions, we obtain the risk-neutral stock and belief dynamics and the European option-pricing equation. Although belief-dependent volatility and the basic option-pricing mechanism are already dealt with in the literature, we derive an explicit leading expansion for conditional risk-neutral log-return skewness. Under the short-time remainder condition in Proposition 5.5 , conditional on p t = p p_{t}=p , and writing σ S ​ ( p ) \sigma_{\text{$S$}}(p) for stock volatility and χ ⁡ ( p ) \chi(p) for the diffusion coefficient of the posterior, we show that Skew t ℚ ⁡ ( τ ) = 3 ​ χ ​ ( p ) ​ σ S ′ ​ ( p ) σ S ​ ( p ) ​ τ + o ⁡ ( τ ) . \operatorname{Skew}^{\mathbb{Q}}_{t}(\tau)=\frac{3\chi(p)\sigma_{\text{$S$}}^{\prime}(p)}{\sigma_{\text{$S$}}(p)}\sqrt{\tau}+o(\sqrt{\tau}). Thus the direction in which a belief revision changes stock volatility determines the leading sign of short-maturity conditional return skewness. When stock volatility is unimodal in the belief, the leading coefficient changes sign at its maximum. This result is an expansion for return skewness; it does not by itself establish the slope of implied volatility. The numerical exercise uses the equilibrium price–dividend ratio and marginal short rate to examine the corresponding finite-maturity implied-volatility curves. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 presents the economy, learning, preferences, financial markets, and the class ℭ \mathfrak{C} . Section 3 characterises equilibrium prices, derives the pricing equation on the belief simplex, and records the resulting uniform bounds. Section 4 studies the two-state pricing equation, while Section 5 derives the physical and risk-neutral stock and belief dynamics and studies European options. Appendices A and B contain the proofs of the equilibrium characterisation and the two-state results, and Appendix C gives the Fourier pricing representation. sections.heading: 2.1 The model
sections.text: Fix an integer n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 representing the number of states of the economy, and use the simplex and differential conventions fixed above. For every initial belief p ∈ Δ n p\in\Delta^{n} , we work on a complete filtered probability space ( Ω p , ℱ p , 𝔽 p , ℙ p ) (\Omega^{p},\mathcal{F}^{p},\mathbb{F}^{p},\mathbb{P}^{p}) carrying a Brownian motion W p W^{p} and an independent right-continuous Markov chain g p g^{p} . The chain has initial distribution p p under ℙ p \mathbb{P}^{p} and takes values in the finite set G ≔ { g 1 , … , g n } G\coloneqq\{g^{\text{$1$}},\dots,g^{n}\} , where the regime-value vector 𝐠 ≔ ( g 1 , … , g n ) ⊤ ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{g}\coloneqq(g^{1},\dots,g^{n})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} has pairwise distinct entries. Its infinitesimal generator is the matrix Λ ≔ ( λ i ​ j ) ( i , j ) ∈ { 1 , … , n } 2 , \Lambda\coloneqq\big(\lambda^{ij}\big)_{(i,j)\in\{1,\dots,n\}^{\text{$2$}}}, where, for ( i , j ) ∈ { 1 , … , n } 2 (i,j)\in\{1,\dots,n\}^{2} with i ≠ j i\neq j , λ i ​ j ≥ 0 \lambda^{ij}\geq 0 is the transition intensity from state g i g^{i} to state g j g^{j} , while λ i ​ i = − ∑ j ∈ { 1 , … , n } ∖ { i } λ i ​ j . \lambda^{ii}=-\sum_{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus\{i\}}\lambda^{ij}. We write 𝔼 p \mathbb{E}^{p} for expectation under ℙ p \mathbb{P}^{p} . Every process and market indexed by p p is defined on this p p -model copy, and all almost-sure, integrability, admissibility, and optimality statements about it are understood under ℙ p \mathbb{P}^{p} . We recall the model of [ 14 ] . For each p ∈ Δ n p\in\Delta^{n} , define the dividend process as the unique solution ( D t p ) t ≥ 0 (D_{t}^{p})_{t\geq 0} of the following stochastic differential equation D t p = D 0 + ∫ 0 t D s p g s p d s + σ ∫ 0 t D s p d W s p , t ≥ 0 , ℙ p –a.s. , D_{t}^{p}=D_{\text{$0$}}+\int_{\text{$0$}}^{t}D_{s}^{p}g_{s}^{p}\mathrm{d}s+\sigma\int_{\text{$0$}}^{t}D_{s}^{p}\mathrm{d}W_{s}^{p},\;t\geq 0,\;\mathbb{P}^{p}\text{\rm--a.s.}, where σ > 0 \sigma>0 is a constant volatility parameter, and D 0 ∈ ( 0 , + ∞ ) D_{\text{$0$}}\in(0,+\infty) . D_{t}^{p}=D_{\text{$0$}}\exp\bigg(\int_{\text{$0$}}^{t}\Big(g_{s}^{p}-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}s+\sigma W_{t}^{p}\bigg),\;t\geq 0,\;\mathbb{P}^{p}\text{\rm--a.s.} Investors observe only dividends, so their information on the p p -model copy is represented by 𝔽 D , p \mathbb{F}^{\text{$D$},p} . They use dividend innovations to update their beliefs about the hidden growth state. For a fixed p p , we denote by 𝒞 p \mathcal{C}^{p} the set of positive, 𝔽 D , p \mathbb{F}^{\text{$D$},p} -adapted and measurable processes. For n = 2 n=2 , this is the hidden-regime learning environment used by Veronesi [ 39 ] and David and Veronesi [ 14 ] : investors observe dividends, infer the current growth regime, and prices depend on the posterior probability of the high-growth state. The formulation above keeps the same economic mechanism but allows for an arbitrary finite number of hidden growth regimes.

sections.heading: 2.2 The dynamics of investors’ beliefs
sections.text: The maximisation problem is a control problem with partial observations because investors do not observe the current growth state g p g^{p} directly. For each p ∈ Δ n p\in\Delta^{n} , let P p ≔ ( P p , i ) i ∈ { 1 , … , n } P^{p}\coloneqq(P^{p,i})_{i\in\{1,\dots,n\}} denote the posterior associated with the law ℙ p \mathbb{P}^{p} . Put differently, P t p , i ≔ ℙ p ​ [ g t p = g i | ℱ t D , p ] , t ≥ 0 , i ∈ { 1 , … , n } . P_{t}^{p,i}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}^{p}\big[g_{t}^{p}=g^{i}\big|\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$},p}\big],\;t\geq 0,\;i\in\{1,\dots,n\}. In particular, P 0 p = p P_{\text{$0$}}^{p}=p under ℙ p \mathbb{P}^{p} . Proposition 2.1 . sections.heading: 2.3 Epstein–Zin preferences in continuous time
sections.text: We fix p ∈ Δ n p\in\Delta^{n} and consider investors with recursive preferences of Epstein–Zin type. The following assumption collects the parameter restrictions maintained in the equilibrium analysis. Assumption 2.2 (Preferences) . Investors discount the future at rate δ > 0 \delta>0 . They have the recursive preferences described below, with relative risk aversion γ ∈ ( 0 , + ∞ ) ∖ { 1 } \gamma\in(0,+\infty)\setminus\{1\} , and an intertemporal elasticity of substitution ψ ∈ ( 0 , + ∞ ) ∖ { 1 } \psi\in(0,+\infty)\setminus\{1\} . The preference parameter θ \theta for early resolution of uncertainty is defined by θ ≔ 1 − γ 1 − ψ − 1 . \theta\coloneqq\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\psi^{-1}}. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, we assume that θ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \theta\in(0,1] . Equivalently, under the preceding restrictions on γ \gamma and ψ \psi , this means γ ∈ [ 1 / ψ ∧ 1 , 1 / ψ ∨ 1 ] . \gamma\in[1/\psi\wedge 1,1/\psi\vee 1]. For an infinite-horizon consumption strategy c ∈ 𝒞 p c\in\mathcal{C}^{p} , the utility process V p , c V^{p,c} should be an ( 𝔽 D , p , ℙ p ) (\mathbb{F}^{\text{$D$},p},\mathbb{P}^{p}) –semi-martingale satisfying V t p , c = δ ​ θ 1 − γ 𝔼 p [ ∫ t + ∞ e − δ ​ θ ​ ( s − t ) ( c s ) 1 − 1 ψ ( ( 1 − γ ) V s p , c ) 1 − 1 θ d s | ℱ t D , p ] , t ≥ 0 , ℙ p –a.s. Formally, it is related to the following infinite-horizon backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) Y t p , c = ∫ t + ∞ F s ( c s , Y s p , c ) d s − ∫ t + ∞ Z s p , c d W ¯ s p , t ≥ 0 , ℙ p –a.s. , Y_{t}^{p,c}=\int_{t}^{\text{$+$}\infty}F_{s}\big(c_{s},Y_{s}^{p,c}\big)\mathrm{d}s-\int_{t}^{\text{$+$}\infty}Z_{s}^{p,c}\mathrm{d}\overline{W}_{s}^{p},\;t\geq 0,\;\mathbb{P}^{p}\text{\rm--a.s.}, (2.1) where the generator F : ℝ + × ( 0 , + ∞ ) 2 ⟶ ℝ F:\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}\times(0,+\infty)^{2}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} is defined by F t ​ ( c , y ) ≔ δ ​ θ ​ e − δ ​ t ​ c 1 − 1 ψ ​ y 1 − 1 θ , ( t , c , y ) ∈ ℝ + × ( 0 , + ∞ ) 2 , F_{t}(c,y)\coloneqq\delta\theta\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}c^{1-\frac{1}{\psi}}y^{1-\frac{1}{\theta}},\;(t,c,y)\in\mathbb{R}_{\text{$+$}}\times(0,+\infty)^{2}, the formal relationship being given by V t p , c = e δ ​ θ ​ t 1 − γ Y t p , c , t ≥ 0 , ℙ p –a.s. , V_{t}^{p,c}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\delta\theta t}}{1-\gamma}Y_{t}^{p,c},\;t\geq 0,\;\mathbb{P}^{p}\text{\rm--a.s.}, which follows from Itô’s formula. Remark 2.3 (Scope of the case θ > 1 \theta>1 ) . Assumption 2.2 restricts the equilibrium analysis to 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 . We nevertheless study θ > 1 \theta>1 later at the level of the Markovian pricing equation. This distinction is necessary because, when θ > 1 \theta>1 , the exponent q = 1 − 1 / θ q=1-1/\theta lies in ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) and the transformed BSDE generator has a continuous extension to y = 0 y=0 for which the trivial zero solution is also available, so uniqueness of the utility process is no longer automatic. An economically meaningful utility process must therefore be selected among its non-negative solutions. Proper-solution selection for related—but different—infinite-horizon Epstein–Zin problems has been explored and developed by Herdegen, Hobson and Jerome [ 25 , 26 ] . Since we do not extend their theory to the present hidden-state model, results stated for θ > 1 \theta>1 concern only the unique positive solution of the Markovian pricing equation. They acquire an equilibrium interpretation only under an appropriate utility-selection rule, whose construction is beyond the scope of this paper. Remark 2.4 (The case θ < 0 \theta<0 ) . sections.heading: 3.1 Main result
sections.text: We use a verification argument to characterise the ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibria for which the representative agent’s value function admits a classical C 2 C^{2} state representation. The class ℭ \mathfrak{C} allows candidate prices to depend on the auxiliary state H p H^{p} and therefore need not be Markovian in dividends and beliefs. The central result of the paper is that this additional state cannot survive in such an equilibrium: every such ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium has a constant auxiliary process H p H^{p} . Consequently, Q p = h 0 ​ φ ​ ( P p ) Q^{p}=h_{\text{$0$}}\varphi(P^{p}) and the stock price is Markovian in ( D p , P p ) (D^{p},P^{p}) . Thus Markovianity is an equilibrium conclusion, not a restriction imposed on candidate prices. The proof of the next result is given in Section A.2 . Theorem 3.1 (Equilibrium characterisation) . Let Assumption 2.2 hold. (3.1) For this ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium, for every p ∈ Δ n p\in\Delta^{n} , on the p p -model copy H t p = h 0 , Q t p = h 0 φ ( P t p ) , S t p = D t p Q t p , r t p = ℛ ( P t p , h 0 ) , t ≥ 0 , ℙ p –a.s. H_{t}^{p}=h_{\text{$0$}},\;Q_{t}^{p}=h_{\text{$0$}}\varphi(P_{t}^{p}),\;S_{t}^{p}=D_{t}^{p}Q_{t}^{p},\;r_{t}^{p}=\mathcal{R}(P_{t}^{p},h_{\text{$0$}}),\;t\geq 0,\;\mathbb{P}^{p}\text{\rm--a.s.} (3.2) Conversely, suppose that there is a constant h 0 > 0 h_{\text{$0$}}>0 satisfying ( 3.1 ), and that the specification in ℭ \mathfrak{C} satisfies h ⁡ ( p ) = h 0 , ℋ ⁡ ( p , h 0 ) = 0 , ℛ ⁡ ( p , h 0 ) ≤ r ¯ ​ ( p ) , p ∈ Δ n . h(p)=h_{\text{$0$}},\;\mathcal{H}(p,h_{\text{$0$}})=0,\;\mathcal{R}(p,h_{\text{$0$}})\leq\overline{r}(p),\;p\in\Delta^{n}. (3.3) Then the specification is a ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium and satisfies ( 3.2 ). Before we continue, let us make two short remarks on Theorem 3.1 . Remark 3.2 (Role of the strict lower bound on ζ \zeta ) . For an arbitrary number of states, the condition min p ∈ Δ n ⁡ ζ ⁡ ( p ) > 0 \min_{p\in\Delta^{\text{$n$}}}\zeta(p)>0 provides the uniform tail estimate used in the proof. In the two-state model with λ 1 2 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$1$}\text{$2$}}>0 and λ 2 1 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$2$}\text{$1$}}>0 , however, this condition follows from the positivity requirement on H H and need not be imposed separately. Hence the necessity conclusion of Theorem 3.1 remains valid without it in that case. A formal statement and proof are provided in Proposition A.3 . Remark 3.3 (Initial wealth and scaled equilibria) . By Definition 2.8 , the representative agent’s equilibrium problem is evaluated at x = S 0 p x=S_{\text{$0$}}^{p} . This initial wealth is the value of the single outstanding stock share. With this wealth, the agent holds that share and consumes the dividend endowment D p D^{p} , so the original economy clears. Figure 1: Twelve simulated paths of the equilibrium ratio in Panel (a) and the corresponding exact conditional means in Panel (b). The ratio remains in [ 7.2 , 9.2 ] [7.2,9.2] . The qualitative conclusion illustrated in Figure 1 is similar to that of the empirical asset-pricing literature: aggregate valuation ratios display persistent but mean-reverting variation; see Fama and French [ 20 ] , Campbell and Shiller [ 10 ] , and Cochrane [ 11 ] . sections.heading: 4 A closer analysis of the Markovian price–dividend ratio for two states
sections.text: In the previous section, the Markovian condition reduced the characterisation of the price–dividend ratio to a scalar nonlinear boundary-value problem. For simplicity, we study the qualitative properties of its positive solution for the particular case of n = 2 n=2 : existence and uniqueness, monotonicity in the posterior belief, and conditional curvature results indexed by the preference-combination parameter θ \theta . The proofs of all results in this section are presented in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 4.3 Monotonicity and curvature
sections.text: We now study the monotonicity and curvature of the price–dividend ratio. Remark 4.9 (Scope when θ > 1 \theta>1 ) . For θ > 1 \theta>1 , the statements below concern the unique positive solution of the Markovian pricing equation. They become equilibrium statements only under an appropriate selection of the recursive-utility solution. Theorem 4.10 (Monotonicity) . Let θ > 0 \theta>0 , let Assumption 4.1 hold, assume λ 1 2 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$1$}\text{$2$}}>0 , λ 2 1 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$2$}\text{$1$}}>0 , and let φ \varphi be the unique positive solution from Corollary 4.4 . Then ( i ) (i) if η > 0 \eta>0 , φ \varphi is strictly increasing; ( i ​ i ) (ii) if η < 0 \eta<0 , φ \varphi is strictly decreasing. Thus the sign of η = ( 1 − γ ) ​ ( g 1 − g 2 ) \eta=(1-\gamma)(g^{\text{$1$}}-g^{\text{$2$}}) determines the direction in which beliefs affect the price–dividend ratio. When η > 0 \eta>0 , assigning greater probability to the high-growth state raises the value of future dividends relative to the current dividend; when η < 0 \eta<0 , the continuation-value effect is reversed. This result is related to, but distinct from, the analysis of Veronesi [ 39 , Proposition 2, see also pages 976–978] . In that CARA model with additive dividends, the stock price is decomposed into an affine present-value component and a negative, convex uncertainty discount, and the resulting equilibrium price is increasing and convex in the posterior belief. Consequently sign ⁡ ( b ) = sign ⁡ ( η ) . \operatorname{sign}(b)=\operatorname{sign}(\eta). The affine form can be compared directly with David and Veronesi [ 14 , Proposition 1(a)] . In their time-additive model, the price–dividend ratio is the posterior-weighted average of the present values obtained by conditioning on each possible current hidden state. It is therefore affine in posterior beliefs. Proposition 4.11 recovers this belief dependence in the two-state, time-separable case. For the curvature result, define m θ ​ ( p ) ≔ c ⁡ ( p ) − α ′′ ​ ( p ) − 2 ​ β ′ ​ ( p ) − θ − 1 φ ⁡ ( p ) , p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . m_{\theta}(p)\coloneqq c(p)-\alpha^{\prime\prime}(p)-2\beta^{\prime}(p)-\frac{\theta-1}{\varphi(p)},\;p\in[0,1]. This coefficient is the zero-order term in the differential equation satisfied by Φ ′′ \Phi^{\prime\prime} , where Φ = φ θ \Phi=\varphi^{\theta} . We now move on to study the curvature of the price-dividend ratio. Theorem 4.12 (Curvature) . Let θ > 0 \theta>0 , let Assumption 4.1 hold, and assume λ 1 2 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$1$}\text{$2$}}>0 , λ 2 1 > 0 \lambda^{\text{$2$}\text{$1$}}>0 , and let φ \varphi be the unique positive solution from Corollary 4.4 . For 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 , Proposition 4.6 identifies it with the equilibrium price–dividend ratio, which is bounded above and away from zero. Because dividend news also changes beliefs, stock volatility depends on the current belief even though dividend volatility is constant. This is the same economic channel emphasised by David and Veronesi [ 14 ] : beliefs about hidden fundamental growth move both prices and future volatility, and this changes the risk-neutral distribution priced by options. Under the standing assumptions of this section, the price–dividend ratio is non-decreasing in p p , so the two channels reinforce one another and learning weakly raises stock volatility above dividend volatility. The proposition above isolates the corresponding infinitesimal log-return effect through χ ​ σ S ′ \chi\sigma_{\text{$S$}}^{\prime} . It does not by itself establish the slope of implied volatility, which is examined numerically below. For the interpretation of the numerical results, a positive implied-volatility slope means that out-of-the-money calls are expensive relative to symmetric out-of-the-money puts, whereas a negative slope means that the puts are expensive. Under the unimodality condition in Proposition 5.5 , the leading return-skewness coefficient suggests the first pattern below p ⋆ p^{\star} and the second above p ⋆ p^{\star} . Whether this prediction persists at a given finite maturity depends on the full option-pricing dynamics. The numerical demonstration below examines this mechanism under the equilibrium calibration. This price statement can be made explicit with a symmetric risk reversal. For maturity T T , define the zero-coupon bond price and forward stock price by ℬ t ​ T ≔ 𝔼 ℚ [ e − ∫ t T r f ( p s ) d s | ℱ t D ] , F t ​ T ≔ 𝔼 ℚ [ e − ∫ t T r f ( p s ) d s S T | ℱ t D ] ℬ t ​ T . \mathcal{B}_{t\text{$T$}}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}\bigg[\mathrm{e}^{-\int_{t}^{\text{$T$}}r_{f}(p_{s})\mathrm{d}s}\bigg|\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}}\bigg],\;F_{t\text{$T$}}\coloneqq\frac{\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}\bigg[\mathrm{e}^{-\int_{t}^{\text{$T$}}r_{f}(p_{s})\mathrm{d}s}S_{\text{$T$}}\bigg|\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}}\bigg]}{\mathcal{B}_{t\text{$T$}}}. For k > 0 k>0 , define RR k ​ ( p , τ ) ≔ σ imp ​ ( k , p , τ ) − σ imp ​ ( − k , p , τ ) , \mathrm{RR}_{k}(p,\tau)\coloneqq\sigma_{\rm imp}(k,p,\tau)-\sigma_{\rm imp}(-k,p,\tau), where σ imp ​ ( k , p , τ ) \sigma_{\rm imp}(k,p,\tau) denotes the Black implied volatility at current belief p p , maturity τ \tau , and forward log-moneyness k = log ⁡ ( K / F ) k=\log(K/F) , with F = F t ​ T F=F_{t\text{$T$}} . Since option prices are non-decreasing in implied volatility, RR k > 0 {\rm RR}_{k}>0 means that the out-of-the-money call with K = F ​ e k K=F\mathrm{e}^{k} is rich relative to the symmetric out-of-the-money put with K = F ​ e − k K=F\mathrm{e}^{-k} . Conversely, RR k < 0 {\rm RR}_{k}<0 is the usual equity-index configuration: downside puts carry the larger volatility and price premium. Figure 5: Equilibrium risk reversals and option premia at τ = 0.10 \tau=0.10 and k ¯ = 0.07 \bar{k}=0.07 . The left panel shows RR k ¯ {\rm RR}_{\bar{k}} computed from discounted option prices, in volatility percentage points. The right panel shows relative wing-price premia, in percent, over a Black price using the same bond price, forward and at-the-money implied volatility. The vertical line marks the volatility maximum. The point p ⋆ p^{\star} should be interpreted as the belief at which instantaneous stock volatility is maximal. It is not, in general, the mean-reversion point of the risk-neutral belief process. The latter is determined by the zero of the risk-neutral drift B ~ ​ ( p ) = B ⁡ ( p ) − χ ⁡ ( p ) ​ λ ​ ( p ) , p ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) . \widetilde{B}(p)=B(p)-\chi(p)\lambda(p),\;p\in(0,1). Thus the leading short-maturity return skewness is controlled by the slope of σ S ​ ( p ) \sigma_{\text{$S$}}(p) , whereas the finite- and long-maturity option surfaces also depend on the full risk-neutral dynamics of p p . This interpretation is consistent with the empirical option-pricing literature. Dumas, Fleming and Whaley [ 17 ] document that implied volatilities vary systematically with strike and maturity, contrary to the flat Black–Scholes benchmark. For broad equity indices, the dominant empirical pattern after the 1987 crash is a negative skew: out-of-the-money puts are expensive because option-implied distributions assign large probability mass to downside tail events; see Jackwerth and Rubinstein [ 28 ] and Bates [ 2 ] . This corresponds in our model to the region p > p ⋆ p>p^{\star} , where bad news raises future volatility. At the same time, order-flow evidence shows that the wing that becomes expensive depends on the market: index option markets are especially sensitive to put buying pressure, while single-stock option markets can be more affected by call buying pressure; see Bollen and Whaley [ 4 ] . Consistently, Bakshi, Kapadia and Madan [ 1 ] find that individual equity option-implied distributions are far less negatively skewed than the market-index distribution. The sign-changing skew in the model should therefore be read as a state-dependent mechanism: the usual index put skew appears in states where downside news increases future volatility, while call-rich surfaces can arise in recovery states where upside news moves beliefs towards the high-volatility region.

Dylan Possamaï Note: ETH Zürich, Mathematics department, Switzerland, dylan.possamai@math.ethz.ch. This author gratefully acknowledges partial support by the SNF project MINT 205121-219818. Mateo Rodriguez Polo Note: ETH Zürich, Mathematics department, Switzerland, mateo.rodriguezpolo@math.ethz.ch. This author gratefully acknowledges partial support by the SNF project MINT 205121-219818. 18 September 2026 Abstract We study a representative-agent Epstein–Zin economy with geometric dividends and a hidden finite-state Markov drift. We allow the price–dividend ratio to contain an additional positive, absolutely continuous valuation factor and, within the class ℭ \mathfrak{C} defined below and under the regularity, admissibility, and positivity conditions of our main theorem, equilibrium forces this factor to be constant, yielding belief–Markovian prices. In the two-state case, under the stated positivity condition and strictly positive transition intensities, we prove existence, uniqueness, endpoint smoothness, interior analyticity, and uniform bounds for the positive solution of the pricing equation. For 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 , this solution supports an equilibrium under any continuous short rate satisfying the model’s one-sided portfolio condition. Finally, in the two-state subregion η > 0 \eta>0 , we derive belief-dependent stock volatility, a European option-pricing PDE, and a leading short-maturity conditional risk-neutral log-return skewness expansion. 1 Introduction Asset prices depend not only on current cash flows, but also on what investors believe about economic fundamentals that they cannot observe directly. When investors learn over time and have recursive preferences, it is not obvious whether current dividends and beliefs are enough to determine equilibrium prices or whether other price components may also arise. We study this question in a continuous-time model. Aggregate dividends satisfy d ​ D t D t = g t ​ d ​ t + σ ​ d ​ W t , \frac{\mathrm{d}D_{t}}{D_{t}}=g_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\mathrm{d}W_{t}, where W W is a Brownian motion, σ > 0 \sigma>0 is constant, and g g is an unobserved finite-state Markov chain driving the different states the economy can be in. The agent learns about the current growth regime from dividend observations. Investors observe only dividends, and thus we write 𝔽 D = ( ℱ t D ) t ≥ 0 \mathbb{F}^{\text{$D$}}=(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}})_{t\geq 0} for the completion of the natural filtration of D D . The representative agent has infinite-horizon Epstein–Zin preferences over consumption. That is, for a consumption process c c , the corresponding continuation utility V c V^{c} satisfies the recursive equation V t c = δ ​ θ 1 − γ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ∫ t + ∞ e − δ ​ θ ​ ( s − t ) ​ c s 1 − 1 / ψ ​ ( ( 1 − γ ) ​ V s c ) 1 − 1 / θ ​ 𝑑 s | ℱ t D ] , t ≥ 0 , V_{t}^{c}=\frac{\delta\theta}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{t}^{\text{$+$}\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\delta\theta(s-t)}c_{s}^{1-1/\psi}\big((1-\gamma)V_{s}^{c}\big)^{1-1/\theta}\mathrm{d}s\bigg|\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\text{$D$}}\bigg],\;t\geq 0, where δ > 0 \delta>0 is the discount rate, γ \gamma is the relative risk aversion, and ψ \psi is the intertemporal elasticity of substitution. Their interaction is summarised by θ ≔ 1 − γ 1 − ψ − 1 , \theta\coloneqq\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\psi^{-1}}, a parameter which will turn out to be qualitatively crucial for our results. Our paper first relates to the literature on learning and incomplete information in asset pricing. Detemple [ 15 ] provides an early general-equilibrium analysis in which investors filter an unobserved state, and Pástor and Veronesi [ 33 ] survey the broader learning literature. Our closest time-additive antecedents are Veronesi [ 39 , 40 ] , and David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . The closest recursive hidden-regime benchmarks are Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] and Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] . Veronesi [ 39 ] studies two unobserved dividend-growth regimes with additive dividends and CARA preferences. The equilibrium stock price is increasing and convex in the posterior probability of the high-growth state. Consequently, bad news in good times has a larger price effect than comparable good news in bad times, while learning also generates belief-dependent return volatility. This belief-driven asymmetry motivates our analysis of the shape of the price–dividend ratio. A closer time-additive benchmark for our pure-exchange and geometric-dividend setting is Veronesi [ 40 ] . That paper considers finitely many hidden growth states under time-additive isoelastic preferences and derives an affine price–dividend ratio in posterior beliefs. Its main question is how the quality of investors’ information affects risk premia and stock-return moments. David and Veronesi [ 14 ] provide the closest pure-diffusion option-pricing benchmark. They consider lognormal fundamentals and finitely many hidden regimes under time-additive isoelastic preferences. Their price–dividend ratio is affine in posterior beliefs, and they show how the common innovation to fundamentals and beliefs generates belief-dependent stochastic volatility, a changing return–volatility covariance, a market price of belief risk, and time variation in option-implied distributions. For two states, they also develop a Fourier option-pricing method. Learning-generated option skews also precede our analysis. Guidolin and Timmermann [ 23 ] derive closed-form European option prices in an equilibrium model in which the probabilities governing dividend news are unknown and updated recursively. They show that Bayesian learning can generate asymmetric implied-volatility skews and systematic patterns across maturities. These learning, volatility, and option-pricing channels are therefore not new to our paper. The second ingredient we use is recursive utility. Epstein–Zin preferences originate with Epstein and Zin [ 18 ] , while Duffie and Epstein [ 16 ] provide the continuous-time stochastic differential utility formulation used here. Weil [ 41 ] and Epstein and Zin [ 19 ] study the asset-pricing implications of separating risk aversion from intertemporal substitution. Epstein–Zin preferences have already been combined with learning about hidden regimes. Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] study a discrete-time Lucas-tree economy with a hidden finite-state endowment regime, Bayesian and distorted learning rules, and Epstein–Zin preferences. Their equilibrium price–dividend ratio satisfies a generally nonlinear expectation equation and is computed as a function of posterior beliefs. Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] consider a hidden two-state economy with an additional noisy signal and focus on how information quality affects expected returns. They obtain the price–consumption ratio w ⁡ ( p ) = ( p ​ w b κ + ( 1 − p ) ​ w r κ ) 1 / κ , w(p)=\big(pw_{b}^{\kappa}+(1-p)w_{r}^{\kappa}\big)^{1/\kappa}, which is also the price–dividend ratio in their endowment economy. Their parameter κ = 1 − γ 1 − ψ − 1 , \kappa=\frac{1-\gamma}{1-\psi^{-1}}, is the counterpart of our θ \theta . They show that this ratio is strictly convex in the belief when κ < 1 \kappa<1 and strictly concave when κ > 1 \kappa>1 . Related work by Ju and Miao [ 29 ] combines learning about hidden Markov growth regimes with generalised recursive smooth-ambiguity preferences. Relative to Veronesi [ 39 ] , David and Veronesi [ 14 ] , Brandt, Zeng and Zhang [ 7 ] , and Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] , our contribution goes in several directions. The continuous-time Epstein–Zin aggregator used here separates risk aversion from intertemporal substitution and leads, away from θ = 1 \theta=1 , to a generally nonlinear pricing equation on the belief simplex. The nonlinearity itself is not new in view of the preceding recursive-utility models. Our first contribution is instead to study whether the belief–Markovian representation used in those models can be obtained as an equilibrium conclusion when a further valuation state is allowed at the outset. More specifically, the earlier papers work with belief-Markovian price representations, whereas we begin with a broader class in which the price–dividend ratio may contain an additional finite-variation valuation state and may therefore retain information about the history of beliefs. We consider a class ℭ \mathfrak{C} of candidate systems which, for every initial belief p p , generate a stock price of the form S t p = D t p ​ H t p ​ φ ​ ( P t p ) , t ≥ 0 , H 0 p = h ⁡ ( p ) , S_{t}^{p}=D_{t}^{p}H_{t}^{p}{\varphi(P_{t}^{p})},\;t\geq 0,\;H_{\text{$0$}}^{p}=h(p), where P p P^{p} is the posterior-belief process, φ \varphi is a positive function on the simplex, and H p H^{p} is a positive, absolutely continuous valuation factor. The term φ ⁡ ( P t p ) \varphi(P_{t}^{p}) captures the effect of current beliefs, whereas H t p H_{t}^{p} may be path-dependent. The class ℭ \mathfrak{C} is broader than a belief–Markovian specification, but it does not contain arbitrary adapted path-dependent prices. The process H p H^{p} must be the unique global positive solution of an ordinary differential equation driven by ( P p , H p ) (P^{p},H^{p}) , and the Borel maps generating H p H^{p} and the short rate are common to all initial-belief model copies. We call a candidate a ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium when, for every p p , the representative agent holds the outstanding stock, holds no risk-free asset in net supply, and consumes the dividend, as in Veronesi [ 39 ] and David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . Our main result shows that, under the regularity, admissibility, and positivity conditions of Theorem 3.1 , including a classical C 2 C^{2} state representation of the agent’s value function, equilibrium eliminates the apparent additional freedom. Even when h h is assumed only Borel measurable, there is a constant h 0 > 0 h_{\text{$0$}}>0 such that h ⁡ ( p ) = h 0 , H t p = h 0 , t ≥ 0 , h(p)=h_{\text{$0$}},\;H_{t}^{p}=h_{\text{$0$}},\;t\geq 0, for every initial belief. Hence, the stock price is Markovian in dividends and posterior beliefs. The belief–Markovian representation used in the earlier literature is therefore an equilibrium conclusion within ℭ \mathfrak{C} , not an assumption. This conclusion is deliberately stated within ℭ \mathfrak{C} : it does not assert that every conceivable adapted equilibrium price, or every solution of an infinite-horizon recursive valuation equation, must be belief–Markovian. This question is related to the literature on existence and uniqueness in infinite-horizon recursive models. More broadly, Santos and Woodford [ 35 ] give conditions that rule out rational asset-pricing bubbles in infinite-horizon economies. Borovička and Stachurski [ 5 , 6 ] derive necessary and sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness in classes of discrete-time recursive-utility and equilibrium asset-pricing problems. Pohl, Schmedders and Wilms [ 34 ] study recursive wealth–consumption ratios, including applications with learning, and select the limit of finite-horizon solutions, which they characterise as the unique homogeneous solution without a bubble. These papers show why the existence of a stationary pricing equation does not, by itself, settle the economic selection problem. Our result addresses a different and more specific question: equilibrium and admissibility eliminate the additional absolutely continuous state admitted by ℭ \mathfrak{C} in the present continuous-time hidden-regime economy. Second, once the belief-Markovian representation is established, we derive the pricing equation for any finite number of hidden regimes and analyse it in detail in the two-state case. The resulting boundary-value problem is degenerate at the endpoints of the belief interval. Under the stated positivity condition and strictly positive transition intensities, we prove existence and uniqueness of its positive classical solution for every θ > 0 \theta>0 . We further prove that the solution is uniformly bounded above and away from zero, smooth on the closed belief interval, and real analytic in its interior. For 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 , the two-state solution supports a ℭ \mathfrak{C} -equilibrium under any continuous short-rate specification satisfying the one-sided portfolio bound. This condition does not select a unique short rate. The direction and curvature of the belief response must also be distinguished. Denoting by g 1 g^{\text{$1$}} and g 2 g^{\text{$2$}} the high- and low-growth states, respectively, monotonicity is governed by η ≔ ( 1 − γ ) ​ ( g 1 − g 2 ) , \eta\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\big(g^{\text{$1$}}-g^{\text{$2$}}\big), the price–dividend ratio is increasing when η > 0 \eta>0 and decreasing when η < 0 \eta<0 . Curvature depends on θ \theta and on an additional sufficient condition. When the latter holds, the ratio is convex for 0 < θ < 1 0<\theta<1 and concave for θ > 1 \theta>1 , while for θ = 1 \theta=1 it is affine without this additional condition. The increasing–convex case echoes the qualitative news asymmetry of Veronesi [ 39 ] , while θ = 1 \theta=1 yields an affine belief dependence analogous to that in David and Veronesi [ 14 ] . As explained above, Brevik and d’Addona [ 8 ] already identify the corresponding preference-dependent change in curvature in discrete time; our contribution is the global existence, uniqueness, endpoint regularity, and shape analysis of the continuous-time degenerate boundary-value problem, together with its connection to the equilibrium-selection result. The maintained equilibrium analysis covers 0 < θ ≤ 1 0<\theta\leq 1 . We do not analyse θ < 0 \theta<0 , which includes the often-used parameter combination γ > 1 \gamma>1 and ψ > 1 \psi>1 . We study θ > 1 \theta>1 at the level of the positive solution of the Markovian pricing equation, but do not provide the additional recursive-utility selection rule required to give those results an equilibrium interpretation. A further related literature combines recursive preferences and option pricing. Garcia, Luger and Renault [ 21 ] develop and estimate an Epstein–Zin option-pricing model with Markov latent variables, stochastic volatility, and time-varying skewness. The state history enters the information set on which their Euler equations are conditioned, so their latent-variable specification is not the same Bayesian filtering problem as ours. Benzoni, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein [ 3 ] study a continuous-time Epstein–Zin equilibrium in which investors update beliefs about a hidden regime governing rare-jump risk. Their mechanism generates changes in stock valuations and in the implied-volatility smirk. Finally, in the two-state subregion η > 0 \eta>0 (equivalently, γ < 1 \gamma<1 ), with the short rate set to its marginal upper bound and under the stated martingale and regularity conditions, we obtain the risk-neutral stock and belief dynamics and the European option-pricing equation. Although belief-dependent volatility and the basic option-pricing mechanism are already dealt with in the literature, we derive an explicit leading expansion for conditional risk-neutral log-return skewness. Under the short-time remainder condition in Proposition 5.5 , conditional on p t = p p_{t}=p , and writing σ S ​ ( p ) \sigma_{\text{$S$}}(p) for stock volatility and χ ⁡ ( p ) \chi(p) for the diffusion coefficient of the posterior, we show that Skew t ℚ ⁡ ( τ ) = 3 ​ χ ​ ( p ) ​ σ S ′ ​ ( p ) σ S ​ ( p ) ​ τ + o ⁡ ( τ ) . \operatorname{Skew}^{\mathbb{Q}}_{t}(\tau)=\frac{3\chi(p)\sigma_{\text{$S$}}^{\prime}(p)}{\sigma_{\text{$S$}}(p)}\sqrt{\tau}+o(\sqrt{\tau}). Thus the direction in which a belief revision changes stock volatility determines the leading sign of short-maturity conditional return skewness. When stock volatility is unimodal in the belief, the leading coefficient changes sign at its maximum. This result is an expansion for return skewness; it does not by itself establish the slope of implied volatility. The numerical exercise uses the equilibrium price–dividend ratio and marginal short rate to examine the corresponding finite-maturity implied-volatility curves.
